definition.title: What Is Character Education?
definition.text: Character education is the intentional practice of helping children and young people develop the values, habits, and social-emotional skills they need to treat themselves and others with respect, make responsible decisions, and contribute to their communities. Through consistent modeling, guided practice, and reflection, character is built not as a single lesson, but as a lived, everyday practice.
definition.followup: MoralEd is committed to making character education a lived, everyday part of every classroom — not an add-on, but a foundation.

about.story_text:
MoralEd was born from a shared belief: that character is the root of lifelong success. Inspired by both global research and local wisdom, we set out to build an educational ecosystem where values are not taught as extras—but lived as essentials.

From its earliest days, MoralEd has stood for more than curriculum. It has stood for culture. For community. For the timeless principles that shape not just students—but societies.
about.mission_lead: To nurture the whole child through culturally grounded, emotionally intelligent, and ethically driven education.
about.mission_body: We empower educators, families, and communities to raise children who lead with integrity and compassion. Our mission is not just to teach values—but to help children live them, feel them, and share them.
about.vision_text: A generation of young people who are not only academically capable, but emotionally aware, socially responsible, and morally courageous—ready to shape a more just and caring world.
about.framework_1_desc: We support academic, emotional, social, and moral growth in harmony.

about.framework_4_desc: We partner with families and communities to make character education real.
about.framework_5_desc: We track growth in empathy, responsibility, and ethical decision-making.
about.beliefs_text_1: Character is universal — it transcends borders, backgrounds, and beliefs, connecting us to our shared humanity. We believe education means more than knowledge: it means wisdom, empathy, and courage, lived in every classroom, not just taught in it.

climate.hero_subtitle: Every teacher knows a calm, connected classroom teaches better than a chaotic one. Here's how character education helps build one.
climate.problem_text_1: When students don't feel a sense of belonging or respect in their classroom, they disengage. Disengagement shows up as disruptions, low participation, and a harder time focusing — not just for the student affected, but for the whole class around them.
climate.problem_text_2: Teachers already know this instinctively: a class that trusts and respects each other simply runs better than one that doesn't. The question is how to build that trust deliberately, rather than hoping it happens on its own.
climate.solution_text_1: Character education addresses the root cause rather than just the symptoms. Instead of only reacting to disruptions after they happen, it builds the shared values, habits, and relationships that make a calm, engaged classroom the default.
climate.solution_text_2: MoralEd's monthly pillars — Respect, Responsibility, Empathy, and others — give students and teachers a common vocabulary for how to treat each other, practiced consistently rather than addressed only when something goes wrong.
climate.related_bullying_text: Left unaddressed, a disconnected classroom climate can escalate into bullying.
climate.related_bullying_link: See how MoralEd approaches bullying prevention
climate.work_1_desc: Every classroom works through the same nine pillars each year, building consistent expectations students can count on month to month.
climate.work_2_desc: Classroom rituals, empathy circles, and activities turn each pillar into something students do together, not just hear about.
climate.work_3_desc: Teacher observations and student reflections give schools a real read on whether classroom climate is actually improving.

research.hero_subtitle: Character education should be more than a feeling — it should be something you can track. Here's how we measure whether MoralEd is actually changing how students treat each other.
research.method_1_desc: Students complete short, age-appropriate reflections at the end of each pillar month, giving teachers a read on how values are landing in daily behavior.
research.method_2_desc: Educators log classroom climate and behavior notes throughout the year, so we can see change over time rather than a single snapshot.
research.method_3_desc: Periodic surveys capture how students and families experience the program at home and at school, not just inside the classroom.
research.method_4_desc: Every partner school receives a summary report translating the data above into clear, actionable takeaways for next year.
research.field_research_intro: MoralEd's approach is grounded in decades of research on social-emotional and character education. Here's some of what the wider field has found — separate from our own program data above.
research.citation_1_authors: Durlak, J. A., Weissberg, R. P., Dymnicki, A. B., Taylor, R. D., & Schellinger, K. B. (2011)
research.citation_1_title: The Impact of Enhancing Students' Social and Emotional Learning: A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Universal Interventions
research.citation_1_finding: A landmark analysis of over 200 school-based programs found that students showed significant gains in academic performance, along with improved social-emotional skills, attitudes, and behavior, and fewer conduct problems.
research.citation_2_authors: Taylor, R. D., Oberle, E., Durlak, J. A., & Weissberg, R. P. (2017)
research.citation_2_title: Promoting Positive Youth Development Through School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Interventions: A Meta-Analysis of Follow-Up Effects
research.citation_2_finding: A follow-up analysis found that these benefits persisted over time, with positive effects on academic performance and social-emotional skills still visible years after programs ended.
research.citation_3_authors: Berkowitz, M. W., & Bier, M. C. (2007)
research.citation_3_source: Journal of Research in Character Education, 5(1)
research.citation_3_finding: A review of character education programs identified consistent practices — including explicit teaching of values, modeling by adults, and sustained implementation — linked to measurable improvements in student behavior and school climate.
research.field_research_disclaimer: These findings reflect published research on social-emotional and character education programs broadly, not studies of MoralEd specifically. We track our own program's outcomes separately, through the methods described above.

bullying.hero_subtitle: Character education works best alongside a clear, honest conversation about bullying — what it looks like, how to spot it, and what to do about it.
bullying.what_intro: Bullying is repeated, intentional behavior meant to hurt, intimidate, or exclude someone who has a hard time defending themselves. It can take several forms:
bullying.form_1_desc: Hitting, pushing, tripping, or damaging someone's belongings.
bullying.form_2_desc: Name-calling, teasing, threats, or insults repeated over time.
bullying.form_3_desc: Deliberate exclusion, spreading rumors, or damaging someone's relationships.
bullying.form_4_desc: Harassment, rumors, or exclusion carried out through phones, apps, or social media.
bullying.signs_title: Signs a Child May Be Experiencing Bullying
bullying.signs_intro: Every child is different, but these are common signs parents and teachers can watch for:
bullying.sign_1: Sudden reluctance to go to school or take part in activities they used to enjoy
bullying.sign_2: Unexplained cuts, bruises, or damaged belongings
bullying.sign_3: Changes in eating or sleeping habits
bullying.sign_4: Withdrawing from friends or family, or seeming anxious and low on confidence
bullying.sign_5: Asking for extra money or "losing" belongings often
bullying.tips_title: What to Do If You're Being Bullied
bullying.tip_1_desc: A friend, a parent, or a teacher — it is always okay to ask for help, and it is never your fault.
bullying.tip_2_desc: Bullying happens less often when you're with people who support you. Look for classmates who can back you up.
bullying.tip_3_desc: Stand tall, keep your voice steady, and say clearly that the behavior needs to stop. Then walk away and tell an adult.
bullying.tips_note: Every situation is different, and there's no single right answer — but keeping it to yourself is never the way through it.
bullying.family_text: If your child tells you about bullying, start by listening without judgment and thank them for telling you. Avoid promising to keep it secret, since adults at school may need to be involved to resolve it. Work with your child's teacher or school counselor on next steps, and check in regularly afterward — knowing someone is paying attention makes a real difference.
bullying.related_climate_text: Bullying is often a sign that a classroom's broader climate needs attention.
bullying.related_climate_link: See how character education builds a stronger classroom climate
bullying.cta_text: Our monthly pillars — including Respect, Kindness, and Empathy — build the everyday habits that make bullying less likely to take root in the first place.

scopeSequence.title: Scope and Sequence
scopeSequence.intro: MoralEd follows a structured, month-by-month character education calendar. Each month introduces a core pillar, a set of related skills, and a clear learning objective your teachers can plan around and measure.
scopeSequence.skills_1: Kindness, compassion, empathy, helping others, mercy
scopeSequence.objective_1: By the end of September, students will practice acts of kindness and demonstrate empathy toward classmates.
scopeSequence.objective_2: By the end of October, students will complete tasks independently and take ownership of their actions.
scopeSequence.skills_3: Respect for self, others, teachers, parents, nature
scopeSequence.objective_3: By the end of November, students will communicate respectfully with peers, teachers, and family.
scopeSequence.objective_4: By the end of December, students will practice honesty and follow through on commitments.
scopeSequence.objective_5: By the end of January, students will apply fairness and inclusion in group activities and games.
scopeSequence.objective_6: By the end of February, students will take initiative in group projects and support teammates.
scopeSequence.objective_7: By the end of March, students will demonstrate resilience when facing academic or social challenges.
scopeSequence.objective_8: By the end of April, students will participate in a community or environmental service activity.
scopeSequence.objective_9: By the end of May, students will set and track progress toward a personal goal.
scopeSequence.age_bands_title: The Same Pillars, Adapted by Age
scopeSequence.age_bands_intro: Every classroom works through the same nine monthly pillars — but how each pillar is delivered changes with your students' age.
scopeSequence.band_1_desc: Picture books, songs, and simple role-play bring each pillar to life through play and repetition.
scopeSequence.band_2_desc: Guided discussions, journaling, and group activities help students connect each pillar to real classroom situations.
scopeSequence.band_3_desc: Case studies, debates, and peer-led projects challenge students to apply each pillar to more complex, real-world scenarios.
scopeSequence.band_4_desc: Independent projects, mentorship roles, and real-world case studies push students to lead by example and apply each pillar beyond the classroom.
scopeSequence.cta_title: See What Comes With Each Pillar
scopeSequence.cta_text: Every month's pillar is backed by ready-to-use teacher guides, activities, and materials.

privacy.intro: This policy explains what information MoralEd collects through this website, how we use it, and who we share it with. If you have questions, contact us anytime at:
privacy.info_text: When you submit our contact form, we collect the information you provide: your name, email address, school name, role (teacher, administrator, principal, or other), and your message. We don't collect this information anywhere else on the site.
privacy.use_text: We use the information you submit only to respond to your inquiry and follow up about bringing MoralEd to your school or organization. We don't sell your information or use it for advertising.
privacy.third_party_text: Our contact form is processed by EmailJS, a third-party email delivery service, which transmits your submission to our team's inbox. EmailJS handles this data according to its own privacy policy. We don't share your information with any other third party.
privacy.cookies_text: We store your selected language (English, Russian, or Kyrgyz) in your browser's local storage so the site remembers your preference on return visits. We don't use tracking or advertising cookies.
privacy.retention_text: We keep contact form submissions only as long as needed to respond to your inquiry and maintain a record of the conversation. You can request that we delete your information at any time by emailing us.
privacy.rights_text: You can ask us what information we have about you, request a correction, or ask us to delete it, by contacting:

faq.hero_subtitle: Answers to the questions schools ask most before bringing MoralEd on board.
faq.question_1: What grade levels is MoralEd designed for?
faq.answer_1: MoralEd is built for K-12 classrooms, with activities, stories, and language adapted to fit different age groups within that range.
faq.question_2: How long does it take to bring MoralEd to our school?
faq.answer_2: Most schools move from an initial conversation to a classroom launch within a few weeks, depending on how much customization and teacher training your school needs.
faq.question_3: Does MoralEd replace our existing curriculum?
faq.answer_3: No — MoralEd is designed to complement your existing curriculum, not replace it. The monthly pillar calendar fits alongside regular classroom instruction with dedicated activities, stories, and discussions.
faq.question_4: What languages is the program available in?
faq.answer_4: MoralEd is currently available in English, Russian, and Kyrgyz, so schools can deliver the program in the language that best fits their students and staff.
faq.question_5: What kind of training do our teachers need?
faq.answer_5: Before launch, your teachers receive hands-on training covering the curriculum structure, classroom activities, and how to track student progress each month. Ongoing support continues throughout the school year.
faq.question_6: How do we measure the program's impact?
faq.answer_6: We provide regular impact reports so you can see how students are progressing across each monthly pillar, based on teacher feedback and classroom observations.
faq.answer_7: Pricing depends on your school's size and the level of customization needed. Reach out through our contact page and our team will put together a quote tailored to your school.
faq.question_8: Can we customize the pillar calendar to fit our academic year?
faq.answer_8: Yes — during onboarding, we work with your school to align the 9-month pillar calendar with your specific academic year and any existing values or themes your school already emphasizes.

activities.topic: What is respect? Respect for parents

items.name: Sorting Game
items.text: Prepare picture cards. Students sort them into two groups. Respectful: helping clean, listening, saying please, sharing, speaking politely. Not respectful: shouting, ignoring parents, throwing toys, interrupting, refusing to help. Discuss why each card belongs in its group.

items.name: Respect Tree
items.text: Give each child a paper leaf and ask: “What is one way you can show respect to your parents?” For example: I listen. I say thank you. I help clean. I speak kindly. I obey the first time. I hug my parents. Attach all the leaves to a classroom tree labelled “Respect Grows Here.”

items.name: Home Challenge
items.text: Create a Respect Chart for one week. Each day students colour a star if they listened the first time, used kind words, helped at home, said “thank you” or cleaned up after themselves. They share their experiences the following week.

samples.story_start_text: Ruby the fox is walking home through the forest when she spots a small leather bag beneath the old oak tree. Inside: a pile of golden coins. No one is around.
samples.story_start_choice_1: 🦊 Keep the coins and hurry home
samples.story_start_choice_2: 🔍 Look around for whoever lost them
samples.story_keep1_text: Ruby tucks the bag under her arm and trots home, already imagining what she'll buy. But on the way, she passes a wooden sign nailed to a tree: 'LOST: A bag of coins, very important to my family. — Mr. Badger'
samples.story_keep1_choice_2: ↩️ Turn back and find Mr. Badger
samples.story_search1_text: Ruby asks around the village and finds Mr. Badger, pacing anxiously outside his burrow. 'I lost my late father's coins,' he sighs. 'They're the only thing I have left of him.'
samples.story_search1_choice_2: 🤔 Mention a small reward before returning them
samples.story_end_reflect_text: Ruby spends the coins, but every purchase feels hollow. She keeps thinking of Mr. Badger's worried face. That night, she can't sleep.
samples.story_end_reflect_moral: Taking what isn't ours might feel easy in the moment — but it rarely brings real peace.
samples.story_end_good_text: Ruby turns around and finds Mr. Badger still searching, tears in his eyes. She hands back the bag. 'I almost kept it,' she admits, 'but it didn't feel right.' Mr. Badger hugs her tightly.
samples.story_end_good_moral: It's never too late to make the right choice — and honesty always feels better late than never.
samples.story_end_reward_text: Mr. Badger pauses, then smiles. 'That's fair,' he says, and gives Ruby a small token of thanks. Ruby feels a little embarrassed for asking, but glad she still did the honest thing first.
samples.story_end_reward_moral: Honesty doesn't mean you can't be treated kindly in return — but the right choice comes first.
samples.story_end_best_text: Mr. Badger's eyes fill with tears of relief. 'You didn't have to look for me,' he says. 'You could have just kept it.' Ruby shrugs. 'It wasn't mine to keep.' From then on, the whole forest knows her as the honest fox.
samples.story_end_best_moral: Honesty and courage — doing right even when no one is watching — build trust that lasts a lifetime.
samples.song_hint: Sing along as each line lights up! 🎤
samples.song_line_1: Small hands can carry big kindness today
samples.song_line_2: A smile, a hello can brighten the way
samples.song_line_3: Share what you have, lend a hand when you can
samples.song_line_4: Kindness grows bigger the more that we plan
samples.song_line_7: One small act can travel so far
samples.song_line_8: Be the kind light, be someone's star
samples.game_perfect: Perfect score! You have a great sense for strong character choices.
samples.game_good: Nice work! You know your values well.
samples.game_grow: Good try! Every quest is a chance to grow — play again to sharpen your instincts.
samples.game_q1_scenario: You see a classmate drop their lunch tray and everyone laughs. What do you do?
samples.game_q1_opt1_fb: That might feel easier in the moment, but it can really hurt someone.
samples.game_q1_opt2: Help them pick it up and sit with them
samples.game_q1_opt2_fb: That's empathy in action — noticing someone's feelings and acting with kindness.
samples.game_q1_opt3_fb: Walking away is easy, but a kind action makes a bigger difference.
samples.game_q2_scenario: You borrowed your friend's pencil and accidentally broke it. What's the best choice?
samples.game_q2_opt1: Hide it and hope they don't notice
samples.game_q2_opt1_fb: Hiding mistakes usually makes things harder later.
samples.game_q2_opt2: Tell them honestly and offer to replace it
samples.game_q2_opt2_fb: Being honest, even when uncomfortable, builds trust.
samples.game_q2_opt3_fb: Blaming others can damage trust and friendships.
samples.game_q3_scenario: Your team loses a game because of a mistake you made. What now?
samples.game_q3_opt1: Quit the team so it doesn't happen again
samples.game_q3_opt1_fb: Giving up skips the chance to grow from the mistake.
samples.game_q3_opt2: Own the mistake and practice to improve
samples.game_q3_opt2_fb: Responsibility means owning outcomes and working to do better.
samples.game_q3_opt3: Argue that it wasn't really your fault
samples.game_q3_opt3_fb: Avoiding responsibility rarely helps in the long run.
samples.game_q4_scenario: You want to try out for something, but you're scared you might fail in front of others. What helps most?
samples.game_q4_opt1: Skip it to avoid any risk of failing
samples.game_q4_opt1_fb: Avoiding all risk also means missing all growth.
samples.game_q4_opt2: Try anyway, even though you're nervous
samples.game_q4_opt2_fb: Courage isn't about having no fear — it's acting despite it.
samples.game_q4_opt3: Wait until you're 100% sure you'll succeed
samples.game_q4_opt3_fb: That moment rarely comes — courage means starting before feeling ready.
samples.game_q5_scenario: A new student sits alone at lunch every day. What would show real character?
samples.game_q5_opt1: Assume they want to be alone
samples.game_q5_opt1_fb: Sometimes people just need someone to make the first move.
samples.game_q5_opt2: Invite them to sit with your group
samples.game_q5_opt2_fb: Simple inclusion can be one of the most powerful acts of kindness.
samples.game_q5_opt3: Wait for someone else to do it
samples.game_q5_opt3_fb: Waiting for someone else means kindness never happens.
